description: Solo B.Tech AI and ML student from Hyderabad building an AI-powered fire safety insights dashboard on NASA microgravity combustion data.
summary: Freefall Fire Insights is an interactive web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion investigations for fire safety in human space exploration. It curates 19 investigation entries - from BASS and Saffire to ACME - drawn from the official challenge statement and NASA's own investigation descriptions, with objectives, test conditions, fuels and source-tagged facts, plus per-card links to search the NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository for the underlying datasets. It ranks investigations for four crew environments (spacecraft and stations, Moon base, pressurized rover, spacesuit) through a transparent scoring model with visible factor breakdowns, and provides SI-drafted, source-linked interpretations, side-by-side comparison and Earth spinoffs. It gathers a hard-to-search archive in one place for students, researchers and engineers studying spacecraft fire safety.
details:
What it does: Freefall Fire Insights makes NASA's microgravity combustion archive explorable. An investigations explorer covers 19 curated entries (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire-I/-II/-III, SAME, SAME-R, DAFT/DAFT-2, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, ACME CFI-G, BRE, E-FIELD Flames, SPICE, SLICE, Flame Design, SoFIE, FLARE, plus upcoming LUCI and FM2) with search and filters by safety area (prevention/detection/suppression), platform, fuel type and status. Each card shows the objective, facility and fuels, sourced key facts, an interpretation, and a link that searches NASA's PSI repository for that investigation's datasets. A habitat ranking view scores every investigation for a chosen crew environment - spacecraft/station, Moon base, pressurized rover or spacesuit - using a fully transparent model (safety-area fit 38%, solid-material relevance 20%, elevated-oxygen evidence 17%, gravity-regime match 15%, direct fire-safety role 10%; upcoming experiments are penalized because their data cannot be used yet). The ranking is a labeled teaching model for relative relevance, not fire-safety design advice. A compare view puts two investigations side by side; an Earth-spinoffs view shows spinoff benefits (smoke detectors, firefighter air tanks and clothing, fine water mist).

How it works: a single-page static web app (HTML/CSS/vanilla JavaScript) with no backend and no accounts; all ranking runs client-side. Quantitative facts are tagged to the NASA source that states them; the ranking weights are hand-set model choices, shown in full, not NASA measurements. An optional Ask SI tab is experimental and unverified: it downloads third-party code and a 609 MB open model from public CDNs to attempt on-device inference via WebGPU. The model download completed, but we could not verify that AI answering works on any device; the feature is prompted but not guaranteed to answer only from the curated dataset, and the rest of the dashboard works fully without it.

Benefits: it gathers the key investigations in one searchable place, makes trade-offs between investigations explicit for different crew environments, and keeps source links one tap away in PSI.

What we hope to achieve: help the Artemis-era community - students, researchers, aerospace engineers - explore and learn from NASA's combustion archive, and recalibrate Moon conclusions when LUCI and FM2 deliver the first partial-gravity data.

Tools: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript; WebLLM (optional, experimental); built with SI (AI) coding assistance.
dataRefs: NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) Data Repository
NASA Spinoff: New Technology for the Fire Attire
